subject: science
title: Chemistry — Earth and atmosphere
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Chemistry — Earth and atmosphere, KS3 Science (National Curriculum).
meta_desc: KS3 Science practice covering Chemistry — Earth and atmosphere, from the National Curriculum programme of study.
final_note: You worked through Chemistry — Earth and atmosphere: 6 programme-of-study statements.

concepts.def: By mass, the Earth is made mostly of the elements iron, oxygen, silicon and magnesium. Iron is the most common element in the whole Earth, because the core is mainly iron (with some nickel).
concepts.specStatementText: the composition of the Earth

concepts.def: The crust is made mostly of oxygen and silicon; by mass, oxygen is its most common element. Smaller amounts of aluminium, iron, calcium, sodium, potassium and magnesium make up most of the rest. Almost all of these are joined together in compounds: the oxygen in rocks and sand is not oxygen gas.
concepts.specStatementText: the composition of the Earth

concepts.def: A rock that contains enough of a metal, or a metal compound, to be worth extracting. Most metals are found in the crust joined to other elements in compounds (often with oxygen); a few unreactive metals, such as gold, are found as the element.
concepts.specStatementText: the composition of the Earth

concepts.def: The thin, solid, rocky outer layer of the Earth, about 5–70 km thick: thinner under the oceans and thicker under continents. It is the coolest layer.
concepts.specStatementText: the structure of the Earth

concepts.def: The layer below the crust, about 2900 km thick: the thickest layer. It is very hot rock that is mostly solid but can flow very slowly over millions of years. Magma forms only where small amounts of rock melt, near the top of the mantle or in the crust.
concepts.specStatementText: the structure of the Earth

concepts.def: The layer around the inner core, made of liquid metal, mainly iron and nickel.
concepts.specStatementText: the structure of the Earth

concepts.def: The centre of the Earth, made of solid metal, mainly iron and nickel. It is the hottest part of the Earth, but the enormous pressure there keeps it solid.
concepts.specStatementText: the structure of the Earth

concepts.def: The crust and the top part of the mantle are broken into a number of huge pieces called tectonic plates. They move very slowly, a few centimetres a year.
concepts.specStatementText: the structure of the Earth

concepts.def: The slow processes by which rocks form, are broken down and are turned into other types of rock. Over millions of years any type of rock can become igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic rock.
concepts.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks

concepts.def: Magma is molten (melted) rock underground. Lava is molten rock that has reached the Earth's surface, for example from a volcano.
concepts.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks

concepts.def: Rock formed when magma or lava cools and becomes solid. It is made of crystals that fit tightly together (interlock). Examples: granite and basalt.
concepts.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks

concepts.def: When molten rock cools slowly, for example magma deep underground, the crystals have time to grow large (granite). When it cools quickly, for example lava at the surface, the crystals are small (basalt).
concepts.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks

concepts.def: Rock made from sediment. Rock is weathered; the pieces are eroded and transported, then deposited in layers. The weight of new layers squashes (compacts) the sediment, and minerals in the water cement the grains together. It often shows layers and may contain fossils. Examples: sandstone, limestone and chalk.
concepts.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks

concepts.def: Rock formed when an existing rock is changed by heat and pressure, deep underground or near hot magma, without melting. Examples: limestone becomes marble; mudstone becomes slate.
concepts.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks

concepts.def: The breaking down of rock where it is. Physical weathering breaks rock up without making new substances, for example freeze–thaw: water in a crack expands as it freezes and widens the crack. Chemical weathering is caused by reactions, for example slightly acidic rainwater reacting with limestone. Biological weathering is caused by living things, for example plant roots growing into cracks.
concepts.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks

concepts.def: Erosion is the wearing away and removal of pieces of rock by water, wind, ice or gravity. The pieces are transported, then deposited (dropped) when the water or wind slows down.
concepts.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks

concepts.def: The remains or traces of a living thing preserved in rock. Almost all fossils are found in sedimentary rock, because the remains were buried in sediment.
concepts.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks

concepts.def: A resource with a fixed amount on Earth that is not being replaced as fast as we use it, so it will one day run out. Metal ores, coal, oil and natural gas are finite: they formed over millions of years.
concepts.specStatementText: Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling

concepts.def: A resource that can be replaced as fast as we use it, for example wood from forests that are replanted.
concepts.specStatementText: Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling

concepts.def: Collecting, sorting and reprocessing used materials (for example melting scrap metal) to make new products. It saves raw materials such as ores and reduces waste, and it usually saves energy. Collecting, sorting, transporting and reprocessing also use energy, so whether recycling saves energy overall depends on these amounts.
concepts.specStatementText: Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling

concepts.def: The layer of gases held around the Earth by gravity.
concepts.specStatementText: the composition of the atmosphere

concepts.def: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide, with tiny amounts of other gases. Real air also contains water vapour, which varies from almost none up to about 4%, so the percentages are given for dry air.
concepts.specStatementText: the composition of the atmosphere

concepts.def: Air is a mixture of elements (nitrogen, N₂; oxygen, O₂; argon, Ar) and compounds (carbon dioxide, CO₂; water vapour, H₂O). Its gases are not chemically joined to each other.
concepts.specStatementText: the composition of the atmosphere

concepts.def: Coal, oil and natural gas, formed over millions of years from the buried remains of living things. Burning them releases carbon dioxide.
concepts.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate

concepts.def: Carbon moves between the air, living things, the oceans and the ground. Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide out of the air; respiration, decay and burning put it back.
concepts.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate

concepts.def: Cutting down large areas of forest. Burning or rotting the wood releases carbon dioxide, and fewer trees remain to take carbon dioxide in by photosynthesis.
concepts.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate

concepts.def: Sunlight passes through the air and warms the Earth's surface. The warm surface gives off heat (infrared radiation). Greenhouse gases in the air absorb some of this heat and send some of it back towards the surface, so the Earth is warmer than it would be without them.
concepts.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate

concepts.def: A gas that absorbs heat given off by the Earth, such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour. Nitrogen and oxygen are not greenhouse gases.
concepts.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate

concepts.def: Extra carbon dioxide from human activity strengthens the greenhouse effect. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC, 2021) states that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land: the years 2011–2020 were about 1.1 °C warmer than 1850–1900. Effects include rising sea level (about 20 cm since 1900), melting ice and more frequent heatwaves.
concepts.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate

mcqs.q: What is the Earth's core mainly made of?
options: Molten rock called magma
The same rock as the crust
Iron and nickel metal
Water at very high pressure
mcqs.specStatementText: the composition of the Earth
mcqs.explain: Yes. The core is mainly iron with some nickel. The outer core is liquid metal and the inner core is solid metal.
rationales: You may have thought the core is the magma that comes out of volcanoes. In fact the core is mainly iron and nickel metal; magma is melted rock that forms much nearer the surface.
You may have thought the Earth is made of the same rock all the way through. In fact the Earth is in layers, and the core is mainly iron and nickel, not the rock of the crust.
Yes. The core is mainly iron with some nickel. The outer core is liquid metal and the inner core is solid metal.
You may have thought the deep Earth is full of water. In fact the core is mainly iron and nickel metal; there is no ocean of water inside the Earth.

mcqs.q: In the Earth's crust, how are most metals found?
options: As lumps or veins of the pure metal
Joined to other elements in compounds
Spread evenly through every kind of rock
As liquid metal that rose from the core
mcqs.specStatementText: the composition of the Earth
mcqs.explain: Yes. Most metals are joined to other elements, often oxygen, in compounds. A rock with enough of a metal compound to be worth extracting is called an ore.
rationales: You may have thought metals are dug up as shiny metal, like gold nuggets. In fact gold is unusual; most metals, such as iron and aluminium, are found joined to other elements in compounds.
Yes. Most metals are joined to other elements, often oxygen, in compounds. A rock with enough of a metal compound to be worth extracting is called an ore.
You may have thought every rock holds the same metals. In fact metal compounds are concentrated in some rocks, called ores, which is why mines are where they are.
You may have thought the metals in the crust come up from the iron core. In fact the core's metal stays deep inside the Earth; metals in the crust are joined to other elements in compounds.

mcqs.q: By mass, iron is the most common element in the whole Earth, but oxygen is the most common in the crust. Which explains this?
options: Most of the Earth's iron is in its core
Most of the Earth's iron is in its mantle
Oxygen gas from the air soaks into rocks
Rusting has used up iron in the crust
mcqs.specStatementText: the composition of the Earth
mcqs.explain: Yes. Most of the iron is in the core, deep inside the Earth. The crust is made mostly of compounds of oxygen and silicon, so oxygen is its most common element.
rationales: Yes. Most of the iron is in the core, deep inside the Earth. The crust is made mostly of compounds of oxygen and silicon, so oxygen is its most common element.
You may have thought the biggest layer must hold most of the iron. In fact the mantle is mostly rock made of compounds of silicon and oxygen; the core is mainly iron and nickel.
You may have thought oxygen is only found as a gas. In fact most of the crust's oxygen is joined to other elements, such as silicon, in the compounds that make up rocks and sand.
You may have thought rusting destroys iron. In fact rust is a compound of iron, so the iron atoms are still there; most of the Earth's iron is in the core.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the Earth's crust is correct?
options: It is the thickest layer of the Earth
It floats on a layer of liquid magma
It is hotter than the rock below it
It is a thin layer of solid rock
mcqs.specStatementText: the structure of the Earth
mcqs.explain: Yes. The crust is solid rock, only about 5–70 km thick. Compared with the whole Earth it is as thin as the skin on an apple.
rationales: You may have thought the crust is thick because the ground beneath us seems so deep. In fact it is the thinnest layer; the mantle below it is about 2900 km thick.
You may have thought the crust floats on liquid magma because lava comes out of volcanoes. In fact the mantle below the crust is mostly solid rock that flows very slowly.
You may have thought it gets colder underground because sunlight cannot reach there. In fact rock gets hotter the deeper you go, so the crust is the coolest layer.
Yes. The crust is solid rock, only about 5–70 km thick. Compared with the whole Earth it is as thin as the skin on an apple.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows the Earth's layers, labelled P, Q, R and S. Which statement about layer R is correct?
options: It is liquid iron and nickel
It is solid iron and nickel
It is liquid rock called magma
It is solid rock, like the crust
mcqs.specStatementText: the structure of the Earth
mcqs.explain: Yes. Layer R is the outer core, which is liquid metal, mainly iron and nickel. The inner core, S, is also iron and nickel but is solid.
rationales: Yes. Layer R is the outer core, which is liquid metal, mainly iron and nickel. The inner core, S, is also iron and nickel but is solid.
You may have thought the whole core is one solid ball of metal. In fact the outer core, R, is liquid metal; only the inner core, S, is solid.
You may have thought the liquid inside the Earth is magma. In fact the outer core is liquid metal, mainly iron and nickel; magma is melted rock, which forms much nearer the surface.
You may have thought the inside of the Earth is solid rock all the way through, like the crust. In fact the Earth has layers: layer R, the outer core, is liquid metal, mainly iron and nickel.

mcqs.q: Lava pours out of a volcano. A pupil says this shows that the whole mantle is liquid. Which statement is correct?
options: The mantle is a sea of liquid magma
The lava rises up from the Earth's core
Most of the mantle is solid rock
Rock gets colder the deeper you go
mcqs.specStatementText: the structure of the Earth
mcqs.explain: Yes. The mantle is very hot but mostly solid rock, which can flow very slowly over millions of years. Magma forms only where a small amount of rock melts, near the top of the mantle or in the crust.
rationales: You may have thought lava shows there is a liquid layer under the crust. In fact the mantle is mostly solid; lava comes from small amounts of melted rock near the top of the mantle or in the crust.
You may have thought volcanoes are fed from the core. In fact the core is metal, far below; the molten rock in volcanoes forms much nearer the surface.
Yes. The mantle is very hot but mostly solid rock, which can flow very slowly over millions of years. Magma forms only where a small amount of rock melts, near the top of the mantle or in the crust.
You may have thought the inside of the Earth is cold because the Sun cannot heat it. In fact rock gets hotter with depth, which is why some rock near the top of the mantle can melt.

mcqs.q: How does sedimentary rock form?
options: Wet mud and sand just dry out and harden
Layers of sediment are squashed and cemented
Sediment melts near a volcano, then cools again
It rises up from deep inside the Earth
mcqs.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
mcqs.explain: Yes. Sediment settles in layers, and the weight of new layers squashes (compacts) it. Minerals from the water then cement the grains together.
rationales: You may have thought mud and sand turn to rock just by drying, like mud in the sun. In fact the sediment must be squashed by the layers above it and cemented together, over a very long time.
Yes. Sediment settles in layers, and the weight of new layers squashes (compacts) it. Minerals from the water then cement the grains together.
You may have thought all rock needs the heat of a volcano. In fact sedimentary rock forms without melting; rock that melts and then cools becomes igneous rock.
You may have thought rocks come up from deep inside the Earth. In fact sedimentary rock is made from sediment laid down in layers on the surface, which is then buried.

mcqs.q: How does metamorphic rock form?
options: Rock melts deep underground, then cools again
Layers of sediment are pressed and cemented
Rain and wind slowly change the rock's surface
Heat and pressure change rock without melting it
mcqs.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
mcqs.explain: Yes. Deep underground, or near hot magma, heat and pressure change an existing rock without melting it. For example, limestone becomes marble.
rationales: You may have thought metamorphic rock forms by melting. In fact rock that melts and then cools forms igneous rock; metamorphic rock is changed while it stays solid.

You may have thought any rock made by pressing is metamorphic. In fact pressing and cementing sediment makes sedimentary rock; metamorphic rock forms when an existing rock is changed by heat and pressure.
You may have thought 'metamorphic' means any change. In fact rain and wind wear rock down (weathering); metamorphic rock is changed deep underground by heat and pressure.
Yes. Deep underground, or near hot magma, heat and pressure change an existing rock without melting it. For example, limestone becomes marble.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows water in a crack in a rock. The water freezes and thaws many times. What is this an example of?
options: Chemical weathering
Physical weathering
Erosion of the rock
Metamorphism by ice
mcqs.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
mcqs.explain: Yes. Water expands when it freezes, so the ice pushes the crack wider; after many freezes, pieces break off. The rock is broken up and no new substance forms.
rationales: You may have thought any weathering involving water is chemical. In fact here the water only freezes and melts; no new substance forms, so this is physical weathering.
Yes. Water expands when it freezes, so the ice pushes the crack wider; after many freezes, pieces break off. The rock is broken up and no new substance forms.
You may have thought breaking rock up is erosion. In fact breaking rock where it is, is weathering; erosion is when the broken pieces are carried away, for example by rivers or wind.
You may have thought any change to a rock is metamorphism. In fact metamorphism happens deep underground, by heat and pressure; ice splitting rock at the surface is weathering.

mcqs.q: Plant roots grow into cracks in a rock. As the roots grow, they split the rock apart. What is this?
options: Not a kind of weathering
Erosion of the rock
A metamorphic change
Biological weathering
mcqs.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
mcqs.explain: Yes. Living things can break rock up where it is. Roots widening cracks is biological weathering.
rationales: You may have thought weathering is caused only by the weather, such as rain, wind or frost. In fact any breaking down of rock where it is, including by plants and animals, is weathering.
You may have thought breaking rock up is erosion. In fact the roots break the rock where it is, which is weathering; erosion is when the broken pieces are carried away.
You may have thought any change to a rock makes it metamorphic. In fact metamorphic rock forms deep underground by heat and pressure; roots splitting rock at the surface is weathering.
Yes. Living things can break rock up where it is. Roots widening cracks is biological weathering.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows layers of rock near the top of a mountain. One layer contains fossil sea shells. What does this suggest?
options: People carried the shells up the mountain
The shells were pushed up from the core
The layer formed from sediment on a sea bed
The layer formed when volcanic lava cooled
mcqs.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
mcqs.explain: Yes. The shells were buried in sediment on a sea bed, which became sedimentary rock. Over millions of years the rock was pushed up to form part of a mountain.
rationales: You may have thought people must have moved the shells there. In fact the shells are inside the rock layer, so they were buried as the rock formed; the rock was later pushed up.
You may have thought rocks and fossils come up from deep inside the Earth. In fact the core is metal, far below; these shells were buried in sediment on a sea bed.
Yes. The shells were buried in sediment on a sea bed, which became sedimentary rock. Over millions of years the rock was pushed up to form part of a mountain.
You may have thought rock layers form from lava. In fact hot lava would destroy shells; almost all fossils are found in sedimentary rock, made from sediment laid down in layers.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows close-up drawings of granite and basalt. Which statement is correct?
options: Granite's magma cooled more slowly
Basalt's magma cooled more slowly
Both are cemented grains of sediment
Both magmas cooled at the same rate
mcqs.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
mcqs.explain: Yes. Granite has large crystals, so its magma cooled slowly, deep underground, giving the crystals time to grow. Basalt has small crystals because its lava cooled quickly at the surface.
rationales: Yes. Granite has large crystals, so its magma cooled slowly, deep underground, giving the crystals time to grow. Basalt has small crystals because its lava cooled quickly at the surface.
You may have thought quick cooling makes bigger crystals. In fact slow cooling gives crystals more time to grow, so granite, with the larger crystals, cooled more slowly.
You may have thought rocks full of crystals are grains stuck together, like sandstone. In fact these crystals grew and locked together as molten rock cooled, so both rocks are igneous.
You may have thought crystal size has nothing to do with cooling. In fact the different crystal sizes show the two cooled at different rates; slower cooling gives larger crystals.

figure.alt: Two square close-up drawings side by side. The left square, labelled granite, is filled by 12 large crystals of different shades that fit tightly together. The right square, labelled basalt, is filled by about 150 tiny crystals that fit tightly together. A note below says both drawn at the same scale.

mcqs.q: Coal and metal ores are called limited, or finite, resources. Why?
options: Only a few countries may mine them
They form far too slowly to be replaced
There is only a small amount of each
Using them destroys the atoms in them
mcqs.specStatementText: Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling
mcqs.explain: Yes. Coal and ores formed over millions of years, far too slowly to be replaced. So there is a fixed amount, and once it has been used it will run out.
rationales: You may have thought 'limited' means only some countries are allowed them, as in 'limited access'. In fact a limited (finite) resource has a fixed amount in the Earth that will one day run out.
Yes. Coal and ores formed over millions of years, far too slowly to be replaced. So there is a fixed amount, and once it has been used it will run out.
You may have thought finite means there is only a little. In fact there may be a lot left; finite means the amount is fixed and is not being replaced.
You may have thought using a material destroys its atoms. In fact atoms are never destroyed: burning coal turns its carbon into carbon dioxide. Coal and ores are finite because they are not replaced.

mcqs.q: Example figures for 1 kg of a metal: making it from ore uses 170 MJ (megajoules). Recycling scrap uses 4 MJ to collect it and 10 MJ to melt it. How much energy does recycling save?
options: 156 MJ
160 MJ
166 MJ
170 MJ
mcqs.specStatementText: Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling
mcqs.explain: Yes. Recycling uses 4 MJ + 10 MJ = 14 MJ. That is 170 MJ − 14 MJ = 156 MJ less than making the metal from ore.
mcqs.working: Energy used by recycling = 4 MJ (collecting) + 10 MJ (melting) = 14 MJ. Energy saved = 170 MJ − 14 MJ = 156 MJ.
rationales: Yes. Recycling uses 4 MJ + 10 MJ = 14 MJ. That is 170 MJ − 14 MJ = 156 MJ less than making the metal from ore.
You may have counted only the energy for melting the scrap. In fact collecting it also uses energy, so the saving is 170 MJ − 10 MJ − 4 MJ = 156 MJ.
You may have thought recycled metal is simply reused as it is. In fact the scrap must be melted, which uses 10 MJ as well as the 4 MJ to collect it.
You may have thought recycling uses no energy at all. In fact collecting and melting the scrap use 14 MJ, so the saving is 156 MJ, not the whole 170 MJ.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a renewable resource?
options: Wood, because new trees can be planted
Aluminium, because cans can be recycled
Coal, because plants keep on growing
Iron ore, because there is so much of it
mcqs.specStatementText: Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling
mcqs.explain: Yes. A renewable resource can be replaced as fast as we use it. New trees can be grown to replace those cut down.
rationales: Yes. A renewable resource can be replaced as fast as we use it. New trees can be grown to replace those cut down.
You may have thought anything that can be recycled is renewable. In fact aluminium comes from ore, which is finite; recycling makes it last longer but does not make new aluminium.
You may have thought coal keeps forming because plants keep growing. In fact coal formed from plants buried over millions of years, far too slowly to replace what we burn.
You may have thought a resource is renewable if there is a lot of it. In fact iron ore formed over millions of years and is not being replaced; there is a lot, but it is finite.

mcqs.q: About what percentage of dry air is carbon dioxide?
options: About 0.04%
About 0.9%
About 4%
About 21%
mcqs.specStatementText: the composition of the atmosphere
mcqs.explain: Yes. Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of dry air, roughly 4 particles in every 10 000. Even so, it has an important effect on the Earth's temperature.
mcqs.working: Accepted composition of dry air: nitrogen about 78%, oxygen about 21%, argon about 0.9%, carbon dioxide about 0.04% (about 420 parts per million in 2024).
rationales: Yes. Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of dry air, roughly 4 particles in every 10 000. Even so, it has an important effect on the Earth's temperature.
You may have thought carbon dioxide is the third most common gas in air. In fact that is argon, at about 0.9%; carbon dioxide is only about 0.04%.
You may have remembered that the air we breathe out has about 4% carbon dioxide. In fact the air around us has only about 0.04%, a hundred times less.
You may have thought carbon dioxide is a large part of the air because it is talked about so much. In fact about 21% is oxygen; carbon dioxide is only about 0.04%.

mcqs.q: Dry air contains nitrogen (N₂), oxygen (O₂), argon (Ar) and carbon dioxide (CO₂). Which describes dry air?
options: A mixture of elements and a compound
A mixture of compounds and an element
Nitrogen and oxygen joined together
A pure substance when it is clean
mcqs.specStatementText: the composition of the atmosphere
mcqs.explain: Yes. N₂, O₂ and Ar each contain one type of atom, so they are elements; CO₂ is a compound. They are not joined to each other, so air is a mixture.
rationales: Yes. N₂, O₂ and Ar each contain one type of atom, so they are elements; CO₂ is a compound. They are not joined to each other, so air is a mixture.
You may have thought N₂ and O₂ are compounds because their molecules have two atoms. In fact each has only one type of atom, so they are elements; only CO₂ here is a compound.
You may have thought gases together make a compound. In fact the nitrogen and oxygen molecules in air are not joined to each other, so air is a mixture.
You may have thought clean air is 'pure'. In everyday language it is, but in science a pure substance has only one substance in it; air has several, so it is a mixture.

mcqs.q: Which statement about dry air is correct?
options: Oxygen makes up about four-fifths of it
Nitrogen makes up about four-fifths of it
Carbon dioxide makes up about a fifth of it
Its nitrogen and oxygen are chemically joined
mcqs.specStatementText: the composition of the atmosphere
mcqs.explain: Yes. Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, roughly four-fifths. Oxygen is about 21%, roughly one-fifth.
rationales: You may have thought air is mostly oxygen because we breathe it in. In fact oxygen is only about a fifth of air; about four-fifths is nitrogen.
Yes. Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, roughly four-fifths. Oxygen is about 21%, roughly one-fifth.
You may have thought carbon dioxide is a large part of air. In fact it is only about 0.04%; about a fifth of the air is oxygen.
You may have thought air is a compound of nitrogen and oxygen. In fact the nitrogen and oxygen molecules in air are separate, so air is a mixture.

mcqs.q: How do greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide, keep the Earth warmer?
options: They let in more of the Sun's rays
They make a hole in the ozone layer
They absorb heat given off by the Earth
They burn in the air, giving out heat
mcqs.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate
mcqs.explain: Yes. Sunlight warms the Earth's surface, which then gives off heat (infrared). Greenhouse gases absorb some of this heat and send some back towards the Earth, keeping it warmer.
rationales: You may have thought warming is caused by more sunlight getting in. In fact greenhouse gases do not let in more sunlight; they absorb heat given off by the warm Earth.
You may have thought the greenhouse effect and the ozone hole are the same thing. In fact the ozone layer absorbs harmful ultraviolet light, while greenhouse gases absorb heat given off by the Earth.
Yes. Sunlight warms the Earth's surface, which then gives off heat (infrared). Greenhouse gases absorb some of this heat and send some back towards the Earth, keeping it warmer.
You may have thought the gases warm the Earth by burning, like a fire. In fact carbon dioxide does not burn; it warms the Earth by absorbing heat given off by the Earth's surface.

mcqs.q: The graph shows carbon dioxide in the air, measured in Hawaii from 1960 to 2020. What is the main cause of this rise?
options: More and more people breathing out
The hole in the ozone layer
Rubbish and litter in streets
Burning coal, oil and natural gas
mcqs.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate
mcqs.explain: Yes. Coal, oil and gas are fossil fuels. Burning them releases carbon that was stored underground for millions of years, and this is the main cause of the rise.
rationales: You may have thought breathing out adds the extra carbon dioxide. In fact the carbon we breathe out comes from food made by plants that recently took carbon dioxide from the air, so it adds none overall.
You may have thought the ozone hole is linked to carbon dioxide. In fact the ozone hole was caused by other gases (CFCs) and does not add carbon dioxide to the air.
You may have thought any pollution, such as litter, adds to global warming. In fact litter is not the cause of this rise in carbon dioxide; burning fossil fuels is.
Yes. Coal, oil and gas are fossil fuels. Burning them releases carbon that was stored underground for millions of years, and this is the main cause of the rise.

mcqs.q: Large areas of rainforest are cut down and burned. Why does this add to global warming?
options: Less oxygen in the air makes the Earth warmer
It makes the hole in the ozone layer bigger
Burning the wood adds carbon dioxide to the air
The heat from the fires warms up the whole planet
mcqs.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate
mcqs.explain: Yes. Burning the wood releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. With fewer trees, less carbon dioxide is also taken in by photosynthesis.
rationales: You may have thought forests matter for climate because they make oxygen. In fact oxygen is not a greenhouse gas, and losing it would not warm the Earth; burning forests adds carbon dioxide, which is a greenhouse gas.
You may have thought cutting forests damages the ozone layer. In fact the ozone hole was caused by other gases (CFCs); forest loss warms the Earth by adding carbon dioxide.
Yes. Burning the wood releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. With fewer trees, less carbon dioxide is also taken in by photosynthesis.
You may have thought the heat of the fires warms the Earth. In fact that heat soon escapes; the lasting effect comes from the carbon dioxide the fires add to the air.

mcqs.q: Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of the air. Can a rise in this small amount change the climate, and why?
options: No, as 0.04% is far too little to matter
Yes, as CO₂ absorbs heat from the Earth
Yes, as it is a poison that pollutes the air
No, as CO₂ does not absorb any heat at all
mcqs.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate
mcqs.explain: Yes. Carbon dioxide absorbs heat given off by the Earth, so even a small rise traps more heat. It has risen from about 0.028% before 1800 to about 0.042% in 2024, and the Earth has warmed.
rationales: You may have thought such a small amount cannot matter. In fact carbon dioxide absorbs heat strongly, so a small rise in it is enough to warm the Earth.
Yes. Carbon dioxide absorbs heat given off by the Earth, so even a small rise traps more heat. It has risen from about 0.028% before 1800 to about 0.042% in 2024, and the Earth has warmed.
You may have thought carbon dioxide warms the Earth because it is a poison. In fact at this level it is harmless to breathe; it warms the Earth because it absorbs heat.
You may have thought carbon dioxide is not a greenhouse gas. In fact it absorbs heat given off by the Earth, which is why more of it warms the climate.

mcqs.q: As the Earth's average temperature rises, which change do scientists expect?
options: Sea level rises as ice melts
Sea level falls as seas evaporate
Earthquakes become more common
Rivers fill up with more litter
mcqs.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate
mcqs.explain: Yes. Ice on land melts and seawater expands as it warms, so sea level rises. It has already risen by about 20 cm since 1900.
rationales: Yes. Ice on land melts and seawater expands as it warms, so sea level rises. It has already risen by about 20 cm since 1900.
You may have thought warmer seas would dry up. In fact the extra water from melting land ice, and the expansion of warmer seawater, make sea level rise.
You may have thought global warming causes earthquakes. In fact earthquakes are caused mainly by movements of the Earth's tectonic plates; they are not an expected result of a warmer climate.
You may have thought global warming and litter are the same kind of pollution. In fact warming does not make litter; expected changes include rising sea level and more heatwaves.

specSource: National Curriculum in England, key stage 3 science — Chemistry; Chemistry — Earth and atmosphere (DfE 2013 programme of study, verbatim)

specStatements.text: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling
the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate

scopeNotes.decision: The composition of the Earth is tested in words: the core is mainly iron and nickel; the crust is mostly oxygen and silicon, with almost all of its oxygen, and most metals, joined to other elements in compounds (metals in ores); iron is the most common element in the whole Earth by mass because most of it is in the core.
scopeNotes.basis: The key stage 3 programme of study says only 'the composition of the Earth'. Accepted values (crust about 46% oxygen and 28% silicon by mass; whole Earth about one-third iron by mass) are used only to say which element is most common. Naming minerals and the chemistry of silicates go beyond key stage 3, and extracting metals from ores belongs to the key stage 3 heading 'Materials'.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item gives or asks for the percentage of an element in the crust or in the whole Earth; elements are compared only as 'mainly' or 'most common'. No item names a mineral or asks how a metal is extracted from its ore.

scopeNotes.decision: The structure of the Earth is tested as four layers: a thin, solid, rocky crust; a thick mantle of hot rock that is mostly solid but flows very slowly; a liquid outer core and a solid inner core, both mainly iron and nickel; temperature rises with depth. Tectonic plates are only named.
scopeNotes.basis: The programme of study says only 'the structure of the Earth'. How plates move and what happens at plate boundaries are taught in key stage 3 geography ('geological timescales and plate tectonics') and at GCSE; seismic-wave evidence for the layers is GCSE physics content.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item asks how or why tectonic plates move, about plate boundaries or about seismic waves; plates are mentioned only in one concept card and, as the cause of earthquakes, in one rationale and one misconception card. No item asks for a depth or thickness: thicknesses in kilometres appear only in concept cards, misconception cards and rationales.

scopeNotes.decision: Igneous rock forms when magma or lava cools and becomes solid (slow cooling gives large crystals, fast cooling small crystals); sedimentary rock forms by weathering, erosion and transport, deposition, compaction and cementation, and may show layers and fossils; metamorphic rock forms when an existing rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting. Weathering is physical (freeze–thaw), chemical or biological, treated in words only.
scopeNotes.basis: The programme of study names 'the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks'; 'rocks, weathering and soils' also appear in the key stage 3 geography programme of study. Identifying minerals, dating rocks and writing equations for weathering reactions go beyond key stage 3.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item names a mineral, dates a rock or uses an equation; chemical weathering is named and described in words only. In the items, concepts and misconceptions on this statement, the only rocks named are granite, basalt, limestone, chalk, sandstone, mudstone, marble and slate.

scopeNotes.decision: Coal, oil, natural gas and metal ores are finite because they form far too slowly to be replaced; a renewable resource can be replaced as fast as it is used; recycling saves raw materials and usually energy, but whether it saves energy depends on the energy used to collect and reprocess the material, judged from given data by addition and subtraction.
scopeNotes.basis: The programme of study says 'Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling'. Life-cycle assessment and calculations of cost or percentage efficiency are GCSE content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The only calculation uses whole numbers given in the stem, labelled as example figures rather than measured values for a named metal, and needs only addition and subtraction. No item asks for a life-cycle assessment, a cost or a percentage.

scopeNotes.decision: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide (about four-fifths nitrogen and one-fifth oxygen), and is a mixture of elements and compounds; water vapour varies, so values are given for dry air.
scopeNotes.basis: These are accepted modern values for dry air (78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon; carbon dioxide about 0.042% in 2024, NOAA). How the atmosphere evolved is GCSE content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: In the items on this statement, the only percentages presented as correct are 78%, 21%, 0.9% and 0.04%, plus 4% for breathed-out air in one rationale; 21%, 4% and 0.9% also appear as wrong values for carbon dioxide and are corrected in their rationales. No item asks about the early atmosphere.

scopeNotes.decision: Burning fossil fuels and deforestation raise the carbon dioxide in the air; greenhouse gases absorb heat given off by the Earth's surface (the greenhouse effect, in words only); more carbon dioxide strengthens this and warms the climate, with effects such as rising sea level. Claims about climate change follow the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report.
scopeNotes.basis: IPCC (2021), Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis, Summary for Policymakers, A.1: 'It is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land.' The carbon dioxide data are NOAA annual means measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii. The evolution of the early atmosphere and carbon-footprint calculations are GCSE content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item asks about the early atmosphere, calculates a carbon footprint or asks students to judge a policy or an opinion. Claims about how human activity is changing the climate, and the effects of that change, follow the IPCC report, and the graph plots NOAA's measured values (rounded to whole numbers).
